description: Somos HORIZON.EXE, un equipo de futuros Ingenieros en Sistemas Computacionales originarios de León, participando con orgullo en la sede de la UNAQ en Querétaro. Para este NASA Space Apps Challenge, nuestro objetivo es desarrollar una vista integrada y multicapa de una ubicación o ruta en la superficie marciana. Al consolidar datos de múltiples misiones científicas de la NASA.
summary:
We developed M.E.I.S , an interactive tactical navigation and telemetry system designed as a Waze for Mars. It features a dual 3D orbital and 2D topographical interface that calculates the most efficient Extravehicular Activity routes for astronauts.

The project addresses the challenge by integrating spatial pathfinding with real-time physiological simulations. Instead of just measuring distance, our custom A-star algorithm dynamically routes around active dust storms and hazardous terrain while calculating actual metabolic drain, oxygen consumption, and power usage based on Martian environmental data.

This system is important because it goes beyond static mapping to prioritize human survival. By continuously monitoring life support systems and automatically redirecting astronauts to the nearest safe refuge when oxygen or battery levels drop below twenty percent, M.E.I.S provides mission control with a vital, data-driven tool to ensure the safety of future planetary explorers.
details:
M.E.I.S operates as a tactical navigation and telemetry system—essentially a "Waze for Mars." It uses a custom A* pathfinding algorithm to calculate optimal Extravehicular Activity (EVA) routes. The system features a dual interface (a 3D orbital globe and a 2D tactical map) and tracks real-time physiological data while dynamically rerouting astronauts around hazardous terrain and active dust storms.

Benefits The system actively prevents life-support depletion and environmental accidents. By continuously evaluating route safety, it can trigger automatic emergency evacuations to the nearest safe refuge (such as Arcadia Planitia or Meridiani Planum) if oxygen or battery reserves drop below the critical 20% threshold.

Intended impact The project aims to provide mission control and future planetary explorers with a robust, data-driven survival tool that tightly couples environmental hazard avoidance with human physiological limitations.

Tools, coding languages, and software used

  • Languages: Python, JavaScript, HTML, CSS, and SQL.
  • Frontend Libraries: Leaflet.js for 2D tactical mapping, alongside Three.js and Globe.gl for 3D orbital rendering.
  • Backend & Data: A custom Python HTTP server, an SQLite database for regional metrics, and direct integrations with NASA Mars Trek for Viking imagery and MOLA topographical tiles.

How the project is creative It merges spatial pathfinding with real-time physiological simulation. Instead of purely calculating distance, the engine computes actual metabolic drain, oxygen consumption (utilizing Weir's equation), and Primary Life Support System (PLSS) power usage based on the astronaut's body/suit mass and the terrain's slope. The inclusion of randomized, dynamic dust storms that force real-time A* recalculations creates a highly immersive and realistic scenario.

Factors the team considered The routing and survival logic strictly weigh a comprehensive set of environmental and biometric variables, including Martian gravity, local atmospheric pressure, temperature ranges, elevation anomalies, regional slope angles, dust storm probabilities, and metabolic energy expenditure constraints.
